title: Debaser
description: The opening blast of Doolittle — Black Francis howling about a surrealist film over Kim Deal's rolling bass line, in the song that taught alternative rock the loud-quiet-loud trick.

pops.text: The whole song is a love letter to Un Chien Andalou, the 1929 surrealist short by Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí.
'Slicing up eyeballs' is literal — the film famously opens with a razor appearing to slice an eye.
Black Francis wrote it while studying in Puerto Rico on an exchange program — anthropology money, surrealist results.
That's Kim Deal on bass and those cool backing vocals, answering Francis's screaming with total calm.
Producer Gil Norton polished the band's chaos just enough for radio on Doolittle, recorded in late 1988 in Connecticut and Boston.
The title: Francis said the film debased morality and standards in art — so the song debases right along with it.
Kurt Cobain openly cited the Pixies' loud-quiet-loud dynamic as the blueprint he was trying to copy on 'Smells Like Teen Spirit.'
Joey Santiago's surf-tinged lead guitar is the sunshine over the violence — a Pixies trademark.
Believe it or not, this wasn't a single in 1989. It was finally released as one in 1997, for the Death to the Pixies compilation — and hit #23 in the UK.
Doolittle is now routinely ranked among the greatest albums ever made. This is track one — some opening statement.

title: Tonight She Comes
description: The Cars' sleek new single for their 1985 Greatest Hits album — Ric Ocasek in full after-dark croon over Greg Hawkes's synth shimmer.

pops.text: This was the one brand-new song on the Cars' 1985 Greatest Hits album — bait for fans who already owned everything else.
Ric Ocasek wrote it and sings lead; the Cars co-produced it with Mike Shipley.
It peaked at #7 on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 1986 — the band's fourth and final top-ten single.
The single's B-side was 'Breakaway,' a track that never made a regular Cars studio album.
That glassy keyboard bed is Greg Hawkes, the Cars' secret weapon — a synth player in a guitar-band world.
Elliot Easton's guitar solo is a masterclass in economy — every note placed, nothing wasted.
Benjamin Orr anchors it on bass. In the Cars, Orr and Ocasek split lead vocals — this one's Ric's turn.
By 1985 the band were MTV royalty, a year after 'Drive' and its award-winning videos made them video-era stars.
The Greatest Hits album itself went multi-platinum — this single helped keep it on the charts for years.
Drummer David Robinson, a former Modern Lovers member, designed the band's visual style as well as its beat.

title: Levon
description: Bernie Taupin's balloon-man saga from Madman Across the Water — a Christmas Day-born pauper, his son Jesus, and Paul Buckmaster's swelling strings.

pops.text: Lyricist Bernie Taupin named Levon after Levon Helm, drummer and singer of The Band — a group he and Elton idolized.
'He was born a pauper to a pawn on a Christmas day' — Levon's father Alvin Tostig names him under a sign from God, in the lyric.
Levon sells cartoon balloons in town. His son Jesus, meanwhile, wants to go to Venus and leave the family business behind.
Released as a single on November 29, 1971, it peaked at #24 in the US — at the time, Elton's second-biggest American hit.
It actually outperformed the album's other single, 'Tiny Dancer,' which only reached #41 on its first run.
Those grand strings were arranged and conducted by Paul Buckmaster, Elton's orchestral right hand in the early '70s.
Madman Across the Water was recorded at the Château d'Hérouville in France with producer Gus Dudgeon.
Elton has described the song simply as being about a guy who gets bored doing the same thing and wants to get away — but can't.
The backing singers include Lesley Duncan, a respected songwriter who appears across Elton's early albums.
Half a century on, 'Levon' remains a fixture of Elton's live sets — one of the deep early songs he never dropped.

title: Possum
description: Phish's roadkill bluegrass-rocker, heard here in the official LivePhish recording from Providence, December 29, 1994 — a founding member's song that became a set-closing institution.

pops.text: Writer credit surprises people: 'Possum' was written by Jeff Holdsworth, Phish's founding guitarist, who left the band in 1986.
The lyric is pure country fatalism: 'I was riding down the road one day — someone hit a possum.'
It first appeared on Junta, the band's debut album, released on cassette in 1988 and reissued by Elektra in 1989.
This version comes from December 29, 1994, at the Providence Civic Center — released in the official LivePhish series.
'Possum' is one of the most-played songs in Phish history — performed well over 500 times across four decades.
It's a set-closer by trade: short, fast and rowdy, built to send a crowd out buzzing.
Allman Brothers drummer Butch Trucks once sat in on 'Possum' with Phish in West Palm Beach in 1995.
Early versions were vehicles for the band's 'secret language' — musical signals that cued the crowd to respond.
Holdsworth returned to guest with Phish decades later, but Trey Anastasio has owned this vocal since the '80s.
Bluegrass bones, rock muscle: the song is a bridge between Phish's bar-band roots and their arena-jam future.

title: Astro Monkey
description: A spacey groove workout from Sweet Oblivious Antidote, the Athens jam band's breakout album — Brock Butler's guitar riding Matt McDonald's swirling keys.

pops.text: Perpetual Groove formed in Savannah, Georgia, in 1997, then became fixtures of the Athens music scene.
'Astro Monkey' comes from Sweet Oblivious Antidote (2003), the album widely regarded as the band's quintessential statement.
The studio cut runs a tight four and a half minutes — live, PGroove routinely stretch it well past ten.
That's Brock Butler on guitar and vocals — the band's frontman and chief songwriter.
Matt McDonald's keyboards give the track its orbiting, space-station shimmer — the 'astro' in the monkey.
Adam Perry's fluid bass is the third leg of the classic PGroove sound, alongside Butler and McDonald.
The band hosted their own festival, Amberland, in Georgia for years — a home base for the Southeast jam scene.
PGroove announced an indefinite hiatus in 2013; Butler, McDonald and Perry regrouped in the side project Ghost Owl.
The hiatus didn't stick — Perpetual Groove reunited and returned to touring, with 'Astro Monkey' back in setlists into the 2020s.
Sweet Oblivious Antidote got a remixed, remastered 20th-anniversary vinyl edition in 2023 — its first-ever vinyl pressing, with two new bonus tracks.

title: Uptown Funk
description: Mark Ronson's retro-funk juggernaut with Bruno Mars fronting the Hooligans — bright suits, city-street strutting and a horn-driven tribute to James Brown, Prince and the Minneapolis sound. The lead single from Uptown Special, it became the defining pop hit of 2015.

pops.text: It started as a jam in Bruno Mars's studio — Mars on drums, Mark Ronson on bass, Jeff Bhasker on synths, and Philip Lawrence trading vocal lines.
That first night produced the opening verse — Bhasker came up with the line 'Michelle Pfeiffer, that white gold.'
Then it took seven months to finish. Ronson has said they kept chipping away, worried nothing matched the excitement of that first verse.
The breakthrough came in Memphis, where Philip Lawrence came up with the 'doo-doo-doo' bass part that Ronson says cemented the whole track.
The video was directed by Bruno Mars and Cameron Duddy, and filmed in part on the 'New York Street' backlot at 20th Century Fox Studios in Los Angeles.
Released on November 10, 2014, as the lead single from Ronson's Uptown Special, it got its first live performance on Saturday Night Live on November 22.
In the UK it was rush-released in December 2014 after Fleur East's performance on The X Factor created huge demand — five weeks ahead of its planned January date.
It spent 14 consecutive weeks at #1 on the Billboard Hot 100 — the longest-running #1 single of the 2010s — and topped the charts in 19 countries.

Its credits grew to 11 songwriters: Trinidad James and Devon Gallaspy for interpolating 'All Gold Everything,' plus the Gap Band team after similarities to 'Oops Upside Your Head' were settled in 2015.
At the 2016 Grammys it won Record of the Year and Best Pop Duo/Group Performance; in the US it was certified 11-times platinum by the RIAA.

title: Cities In Dust
description: Siouxsie's dancefloor elegy for Pompeii — the lead single from Tinderbox, all chiming guitars, DX7 shimmer and volcanic dread.

pops.text: The song is about Pompeii — the Roman city buried by Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD. 'Your city lies in dust, my friend.'
Released in October 1985 as the lead single from Tinderbox, it reached #21 in the UK.
In America it became a club hit, climbing to #17 on the Billboard dance chart — the Banshees' US breakthrough.
It was the band's first single with guitarist John Valentine Carruthers as a full member.
Tinderbox was recorded at Hansa Tonstudio in Berlin in May 1985 — the studio made famous by Bowie and Iggy Pop.
Those cavernous keyboard textures come from bassist Steven Severin's new Yamaha DX7, a 1985 studio staple.
Siouxsie, Severin, drummer Budgie and Carruthers share the songwriting credit — and the band produced Tinderbox themselves.
The single's B-sides were 'An Execution' and the wonderfully titled 'Quarterdrawing of a Dog.'
Pompeii's plaster casts of the victims haunted Siouxsie — the lyric addresses the dead directly, as 'my friend.'
It remains one of the Banshees' signature songs — goth turning, defiantly, toward the dancefloor.

title: Rhiannon
description: Stevie Nicks's Welsh-witch invocation, performed live in 1976 — the song that announced the new Fleetwood Mac and made Nicks a star.

pops.text: Stevie Nicks wrote 'Rhiannon' in 1974, before she joined Fleetwood Mac — it was meant for a second Buckingham Nicks album.
The spark was a novel: Triad by Mary Bartlet Leader, about a woman possessed by the spirit of a witch named Rhiannon.
Only later did Nicks learn Rhiannon is a real figure of Welsh mythology, from the medieval Mabinogion tales.
On stage, Nicks introduced it for years as 'a song about an old Welsh witch' — then sang like she was possessed herself.
This performance was filmed live at Studio Instrument Rentals in 1976, as the song was climbing the charts.
Released as a single in 1976 under the fuller title 'Rhiannon (Will You Ever Win),' it peaked at #11 on the Hot 100.
The album version was recorded at Sound City in Los Angeles with producer Keith Olsen — the man who brought Buckingham and Nicks into the band.
That hypnotic drum pattern was partly a studio construction — Olsen spliced Mick Fleetwood's takes together on tape to get the loop-like feel.
Nicks sang it so hard in the early years that she sometimes damaged her voice and forced dates to be rescheduled.
Rolling Stone placed 'Rhiannon' on its list of the 500 greatest songs of all time — the White Witch endures.

title: Cantaloupe Island
description: Herbie's immortal 16-bar groove from Empyrean Isles — four masters, one June day at Rudy Van Gelder's studio, and a melody every jam session on Earth still calls.

pops.text: Recorded on June 17, 1964, at Van Gelder Studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, for Blue Note Records.
The band is a dream team: Freddie Hubbard on cornet, Ron Carter on bass, and Tony Williams — just 18 years old — on drums.
Hancock was simultaneously the pianist in Miles Davis's Second Great Quintet — Carter and Williams were his bandmates there too.
The whole tune is a compact 16-bar form in F minor — four chords' worth of harmony, endlessly loopable.
It's from Empyrean Isles, Hancock's fourth Blue Note album, produced by label founder Alfred Lion.
The tune became a certified jazz standard — recorded well over 95 times by other artists.
Nearly 30 years later, British group US3 sampled this groove for their 1993 hit 'Cantaloop (Flip Fantasia).'
US3's sample carried Hancock's piano to the pop top ten — and introduced a new generation to Blue Note.
Hancock re-recorded the tune himself more than once, including a solo piano version on his album Dedication.
Simple, funky and modal all at once — critics call it the perfect convergence of hard bop, soul jazz and modal jazz.

title: Your House
description: Birmingham's reggae revolutionaries soften into a lovers' plea — the beloved love song from True Democracy, Steel Pulse's first album for Elektra.

pops.text: Steel Pulse formed in the Handsworth district of Birmingham, England, in 1975 — British reggae's great roots band.
'Your House' comes from True Democracy (1982), the band's first album for Elektra Records.
The album was recorded in 1981 at Feedback Studios in Denmark, with producer Karl Pitterson.
Founder and frontman David Hinds sings lead — a straight-up love song from a band famous for militant politics.
True Democracy marked a brighter, more buoyant, pop-inflected sound than the edgy roots of Handsworth Revolution.
The core lineup here: Hinds, Selwyn Brown on keys and vocals, Basil Gabbidon on guitar, Ronnie McQueen on bass and Steve Nisbett on drums.
Five years later the band won the Grammy for Best Reggae Album with Babylon the Bandit — the first non-Jamaican band ever to win a reggae Grammy.
'Your House' became one of the band's signature songs, a permanent encore fixture in their live sets.
The band's name was borrowed from a racehorse — a stud farm's prizewinner, if the old story is told right.
Still touring half a century on, Steel Pulse remain the standard-bearers of British roots reggae.

title: Scar Tissue
description: The Chili Peppers, bloodied but rolling through the desert in a battered car — Stéphane Sednaoui's sun-bleached video for the Californication comeback single.

pops.text: Released May 25, 1999, as the first single from Californication — the album that reunited the band with guitarist John Frusciante.
Frusciante had been gone for six years. His return — and his slide-guitar solo here — powered the band's second act.
The video was directed by Stéphane Sednaoui, who'd also directed the band's breakthrough 'Give It Away' clip.
The concept is a desert road trip: all four members, bandaged and bruised, piled into a wreck of a car. Scar tissue, visualized.
It hit #9 on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped both the Mainstream Rock and Modern Rock charts.
At the 2000 Grammys, 'Scar Tissue' won Best Rock Song.
Producer Rick Rubin kept the arrangement bare — the warmth is Frusciante's guitar and Anthony Kiedis's most melodic vocal yet.
Kiedis later took the title for his 2004 memoir, Scar Tissue — one of rock's bestselling autobiographies.
All four members share the songwriting credit: Flea, Frusciante, Kiedis and drummer Chad Smith.
Californication went on to sell over 15 million copies — this gentle song, not a funk workout, led the charge.

title: Graceland
description: Paul Simon's pilgrimage song — a drive to Elvis's Memphis mansion with South African guitars, the Everly Brothers on harmony, and a heart still mid-divorce.

pops.text: The title track of Simon's 1986 masterpiece — an album built from sessions with South African musicians in Johannesburg.
Listen for the harmonies: that's the Everly Brothers, Don and Phil, singing behind Simon.
The liquid fretless bass is Bakithi Kumalo, whose playing became the Graceland album's signature sound.
Simon really made the drive — he travelled to Graceland, Elvis Presley's Memphis home, with his young son in mind for the lyric.
'Poor boys and pilgrims with families' — the song frames the trip as a pilgrimage for the broken-hearted.
The opening lines — 'The Mississippi Delta was shining like a National guitar' — are among Simon's most quoted.
As a single it only reached #81 in the US in late 1986. The album it named became a phenomenon anyway.
The Graceland album won the Grammy for Album of the Year in 1987.
And this title song won its own Grammy — Record of the Year — the following year, in 1988.
Guitarist Ray Phiri and drummer Vusi Khumalo lead the South African rhythm engine under Simon's very American song.

title: Tunnel of Love
description: Bruce walks a darkened Asbury Park fairground in Neil Jordan's video — love as a rigged carnival ride, from the most introspective album of his career.

pops.text: The title track of Springsteen's 1987 album Tunnel of Love — his quiet, synth-lit follow-up to the Born in the U.S.A. blockbuster.
The video was directed by Irish filmmaker Neil Jordan, director of Mona Lisa and later The Crying Game.
It was shot at a shuttered fairground in Asbury Park, New Jersey — Bruce's spiritual home turf, gone to seed.
The video earned five MTV Video Music Award nominations, including Video of the Year.
The single peaked at #13 on the Billboard Hot 100 in late 1987.
Unlike the E Street records, Bruce recorded this album mostly alone, bringing band members in one at a time for overdubs.
You can hear Nils Lofgren's guitar, Roy Bittan's synthesizer and Max Weinberg's percussion — plus backing vocals from Patti Scialfa.
Scialfa later became Springsteen's wife; the album's songs about a failing marriage were written as his first marriage was ending.
Bruce has said that after 20 years writing about the man on the road, this album was about 'the man in the house.'
The carnival metaphor does the heavy lifting: the tunnel of love is funhouse-scary, and the ride is rigged to separate you.

title: Blitzkrieg Bop
description: Hey ho, let's go — two minutes and change that launched punk rock, from the Ramones' 1976 debut, all leather jackets, downstrokes and a chant for the ages.

pops.text: 'Hey ho, let's go!' — drummer Tommy Ramone modeled the chant on the Bay City Rollers' 'Saturday Night.'
Tommy wrote most of the song, with bassist Dee Dee Ramone contributing — it was originally titled 'Animal Hop.'
Released in February 1976, it was the Ramones' debut single — and track one of their debut album that April.
The debut album famously cost about $6,400 to record, cut quickly at Plaza Sound in New York with producer Craig Leon.
Johnny Ramone's guitar is all downstrokes, all the time — the Mosrite-driven blur that defined punk guitar.
The four members weren't brothers and weren't named Ramone — the name nods to Paul McCartney's old stage name, Paul Ramon.
Joey Ramone — born Jeffrey Hyman — stood 6'6" and sang the whole thing in a joyful, adenoidal croon.
It never charted on release. Punk rarely did. It became an anthem the slow way — through every kid who ever heard it.
A new generation met it in Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017), where it soundtracks Peter Parker's sprint home.
Rolling Stone ranks it among the greatest songs of all time — 2 minutes, 12 seconds, zero wasted motion.

title: Let's Groove
description: Earth, Wind & Fire answer the 'disco is dead' crowd with vocoders, video-game graphics and the funkiest invitation of 1981 — the lead single from Raise!

pops.text: That robotic voice at the top is a vocoder — Maurice White answering disco's backlash with pure early-'80s technology.
'Let's Groove' was the first single from Raise! (1981), written by Maurice White with Wayne Vaughn.
It spent five weeks at #1 on the Hot Soul Singles chart and peaked at #3 on the Billboard Hot 100.
The video was a pioneer — its early computer-style graphics and effects made it a favorite of the brand-new MTV era.
Maurice White produced it, layering horns, synth bass, Rhodes piano and those stereo handclaps onto 24 tracks of tape.
Drummer Fred White — Maurice's half-brother — lays down the pocket the whole groove rides on.
Philip Bailey shares the vocal spotlight, trading lines with Maurice over Verdine White's dancing bass.
The song won the Grammy for Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal.
Raise! went platinum and its cover — a futuristic Egyptian scene by artist Shusei Nagaoka — continued the band's cosmic visual saga.
Four decades on, it's a wedding, TikTok and roller-rink immortal — the groove never actually stopped.
